newsitem.title: UK: IBCA raises Uruguay rating to investment grade.
newsitem.headline: IBCA raises Uruguay rating to investment grade.

text.p: European credit rating agency IBCA on Thursday awarded Uruguay a BBB-minus credit rating for its long-term foreign currency debt, making it only the third Latin American country to win the coveted investment grade.
An investment grade rating allows the country to borrow more cheaply on the international capital markets, while increasing the number of U.S. funds that are permitted to buy its debt.
"IBCA...has assigned a BBB-minus long term foreign currency rating to the Oriental Republic of Uruguay," the agency said in a statement released in London.
Elsewhere in Latin America only Chile and Colombia have won this market cachet. Colombia is rated A-plus by Standard and Poor's and Chile is rated BAA1 by Moody's Investors Service.

IBCA, which also upgraded Uruguay's short-term foreign currency rating to A3 from B, cited the significant progress the country has made in fiscal consolidation, which has underpinned its stabilisation programme and led to a steady reduction in inflation.
It also praised Uruguay's efforts to reform its pension system.

"The pension reform removes a worry about the long-term sustainability of fiscal adjustment, and will underpin growth of national savings and investment, and help the economy become less reliant on foreign capital inflows," it said.
The agency said Uruguay had performed well in the aftermath of the 1994-5 Mexican financial crisis which threatened to destabilise much of Latin America.

"The post-Mexico crisis showed that Uruguay's position as a regional banking centre and recipient of capital flight puts it in an advantageous position even during a severe regional stress test," it said.
IBCA said the speed of structural reform in Uruguay was likely to accelerate because of changes in its political system.

"Results of the December 1996 referendum herald changes to the electoral law which should discourage the factionalism that hitherto has characterised Uruguayan political life," it said, adding this should promote more cohesive parties, governments and policy-making.
However IBCA said there were also a number constraints on the country's rating.
It cited worries over adjustment to economic liberalisation entailed by its membership of regional trade bloc Mercosur, and the sedate pace of reform to date.
Mercosur groups Uruguay with Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay, and has Chile as an associate partner.
